Senses.Explanation: The eye of heaven and earth is a public case phrase asked directly of Jiufeng Daoqian and raised in Zhaozhou's claim to hold that eye fast without leaking the slightest thread. An unnamed questioner asks Jiufeng what the eye is. Jiufeng first places heaven and earth within it, then answers that this itself is the eye, and says its illumination does not borrow the power of sun, moon, or stars. Later collections repeatedly reopen each turn rather than paraphrase the answer away. Zhaozhou's separate formula says he holds fast the eye of heaven and earth without leaking the slightest amount and demands that the audience understand. Wansong Xingxiu tests whether this has truly been settled and warns that even a penetrating answer can remain inside Zhaozhou's enclosure.

Linji Yixuan asks what dry shit-stick the person of no rank is; Deshan Xuanjian predicates it of old Shakyamuni; and Yunmen Wenyan asks what dry shit-stick an assembly seeks to chew. In Yunmen’s famous case it answers ‘What is Buddha?’ Wumen Huikai preserves Yunmen as the answerer, Dahui Zonggao repeats the case in verse, and Zhongfeng Mingben places it beside the courtyard cypress and three catties of hemp as sayings with no route for explanatory boring. Senses.Explanation: The line enters the record as the visiting monk Zun Buna's boast in a verse duel at the foot of Shaoshan: asked to show his house style, he answers that one phrase leaps past a thousand sages — the old-man's-beard lichen draped on the pines does not rank with the moon disc — and the old master Shaoshan Huanpu caps him at once: grant that you shoot straight past the Sound-of-Awe awakening, you are still half a month short of Shaoshan. The Jingde lamp of 1004 carries the duel in its life of Shaoshan, which closes on his posthumous title Wuwei. Dahui Zonggao retold the duel whole in his Zhengfayan zang and ended on his own verdict — venerable Chen of Muzhou would laugh himself dead. Linquan Conglun set it as the thirteenth case of his Empty Valley Collection and ruled that Shaoshan's old man is used to facing great enemies, while the questioner was softly covered by one white cloud; Touzi Yiqing versified it. At a court sitting in 1101 the Jinshan master Fojian Weizhong heard an unnamed monk offer the couplet at the empress's incense embassy and capped it: once understood here, seek it nowhere else. The later masters spent the couplet as ready currency: Shanhui Huan capped a hall address with it, Mingjue Cong answered a pressing layman with it, Xisou Shaotan closed a retreat talk on it after swapping out the first hemistich, and Hansong Zhicao answered his teacher with it — Baiyu Jingsi called it a somersault in the vines, then told the assembly that questioning should look like this. The root transmission is the Jingde lamp's life of Shaoshan Huanpu of Luojing: the direction question at the foot of the mountain, the green-bamboo answer, the archery couplets, the headword as the visiting monk's boast — this lamp reading the first hemistich as past-and-present — the half-month retort, and the fault question answered as untrammeled wording that people know. Dahui Zonggao retold the duel whole in his Zhengfayan zang, through the closing dare of sky-soaring breath against earth-burrowing stratagem, the bright mirror refused because fish will not bite in shallow water, and the staff-blow, then delivered his own verdict under his studio name Miaoxi: venerable Chen of Muzhou would laugh himself dead. The commentators made the duel bear their verdicts. Linquan Conglun set it as the thirteenth case of the Empty Valley Collection, framed by the old case of the white cloud that shows no ugliness; his verdict holds this was no small power — Shaoshan's old man is used to facing great enemies and does not fear a spent force — while the questioner came pressing with idle right-and-wrong and was softly covered by one white cloud; the rest of the flavor, he says, he hands to Touzi. Touzi Yiqing's verse opens on the white cloud that never reaches the central peak, the scene of hanging mist apart, one tune cold through a thousand ages, ten thousand folds of green under the moon just risen. The later masters spent the couplet as live currency. Shanhui Huan capped a hall address with it — this matter needs no raising when we meet, the white horse with gold saddle fords the willow stream, then the headword line. Mingjue Cong, pressed by the layman Zhou to speak one phrase with throat and lips shut and outside thought and knowledge, answered with the couplet and opened his address on the Yanguan drum. Xisou Shaotan closed his retreat-opening talk on it after replacing the first hemistich with his own going free and alone past a thousand miles — keeping the headword as the fixed member. Hansong Zhicao answered his teacher's hooks-and-nets image with it; Baiyu Jingsi retorted that it too is a somersault in the vines, Hansong Zhicao shouted once and left, and Baiyu Jingsi told the assembly that questioning should look like this. At the court sitting of the thirteenth day of the fourth month of 1101, recorded in the Jianzhong Jingguo Continued Lamp Record's life of the Jinshan master Fojian Weizhong, the empress's incense embassy came for the first-year rite of the prince the Duke of Han; after the opening exchange an unnamed monk offered the headword couplet as his ceremonial line, and the presiding master capped it — once understood here, do not pursue it elsewhere — before the censer and wooden-man exchanges closed the sitting.

Senses.Explanation: Hundreds, thousands, myriads, and millions is an emphatic number governed by its counted noun. At an offering for the birthday of the venerable Huanyou, Yulin Tongxiu points to the portrait and says that the old man sitting there leaves everyone at a loss, habitually gains the advantage, and that anyone who passes through here is like a dragon finding water or a tiger leaning on a mountain, adding vigor where there is vigor and style where there is none. The expression is therefore an emphatic count governed by descendants.

Senses.Explanation: How do you advance from the top of a hundred-foot pole? asks for movement from a place where ordinary footing has apparently run out. An unnamed monk puts the question to Fayun Datong Shanben, who answers ‘danger’ and, when pressed, ‘shattered to pieces.’ Chuiwan Guangzhen later raises Changsha Jingcen’s exchange and supplies his own road answer to a prospective questioner. Another record places Qingliang Taiqin’s one-syllable answer inside the inquiry that Chaling Yushan Zhu sustained until his bridge fall, while Tianyin Yuanxiu tells his questioner to look behind and then come forward. Wumen Huikai also transmits the question under Shishuang’s name. These answers test the same literal question; they do not establish one prescribed next step or several meanings for the words.

Senses.Explanation: Smashed into a hundred fragments says that something has been broken beyond recovery rather than corrected or polished. Guanghui Lian imagines a toad or earthworm leaping into Mount Sumeru and smashing it to fragments, then drives the assembly out with his staff. Layman Pang Yun answers Damei Fachang's question about where to bite a ripe plum with the same phrase; Damei asks him to return the pit. Xisou Shaotan strikes the spring ox into fragments, while Shexian Guisheng answers ‘the adamantine body’ with ‘a hundred fragments’ and follows it with ‘in the end, one heap of ash.’ An unnamed elder says Tangchaoyin's single strike shattered the mountains and earth; Touzi Yiqing raises his staff and pronounces the same verdict. The phrase keeps its violent force, but the target is supplied by each encounter.

Senses.Explanation: Zhong Kui is the demon-quelling figure invoked in public answers and Double-Fifth festival addresses. Wuzu Fayan uses the name in two different answers, Huiyue Xu describes the sight of Zhong Kui as destructive to little ghosts, and Mingjue Cong pictures him holding an iron brush while protective writing appears on household doors. Dongshan Shouchu also gives the unglossed answer that Zhong Kui does not read books. The passages use the familiar named figure without assigning a further symbolic meaning.
